record.title: SELF-INDEX reports search and memory retrieval gains from revisable keys
record.summary: The authors of SELF-INDEX describe an optimizer that diagnoses retrieval shortfalls, revises document keys, validates changes and uses simulated queries. Their paper reports improvements across BRIGHT with three retrievers, BrowseComp-Plus across four backbones and LongMemEval V2. For GPT-OSS-120B with BM25, reported BrowseComp-Plus accuracy rises from 31.08% to 58.92% while search calls decrease. LongMemEval results vary by task: several improve by 9.2–13.9%, while Gotchas is unchanged or lower. These are paper-reported results; independent replication and matched full optimization-cost comparisons remain open.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that SELF-INDEX improves BRIGHT retrieval across three retrievers and BrowseComp-Plus search across four backbones, with fewer search calls in reported configurations. On GPT-OSS-120B with BM25, BrowseComp-Plus accuracy increases from 31.08% to 58.92%.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On LongMemEval V2, the authors report gains of 9.2–13.9% on several tasks; the task-specific Gotchas result is unchanged or lower, so the reported effect is not uniform.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The reported evaluations are author-run; simulated optimization queries are used, and this review did not independently reproduce the results or establish a matched total index-construction and inference-cost comparison.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the reported retrieval and search-agent gains was found in this review.
Reported search-token use does not establish total optimization and index-construction cost relative to a fixed-index baseline under an equalized end-to-end budget.

brief.importance_rationale: If revisable retrieval keys reliably improve search and long-term memory under equalized total cost, the method could improve retrieval-augmented agents across domains. A 5 reflects broad but bounded potential; current evidence is a multi-task author report with variable task outcomes and unresolved end-to-end optimization cost.
limitations: All quantitative results cited here are reported by the authors and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
Search-call or retrieval gains do not by themselves establish lower total compute or latency because optimization and index-construction costs must be included.
Performance varies by task; the reported LongMemEval Gotchas result is unchanged or lower.

technical.claimed_result: Author-reported BRIGHT, BrowseComp-Plus and LongMemEval V2 results. For GPT-OSS-120B+BM25, BrowseComp-Plus accuracy is reported as 31.08% to 58.92% with fewer search calls; LongMemEval gains vary by task.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports token usage and search calls, but this review did not establish equalized total cost including query simulation and index construction.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper describes a concrete optimizer loop that diagnoses retrieval failures, revises document keys and validates candidate changes. Quantitative outcomes remain author-reported.
technical.implementation_status: Research prototype described in the arXiv paper; the authors provide a public implementation link.
technical.mechanism: An optimizer uses simulated queries to identify retrieval failures, revises keys for relevant documents and checks whether proposed revisions improve retrieval before retaining them.
technical.regime: Author-run experiments on BRIGHT, BrowseComp-Plus and LongMemEval V2 using multiple retrievers/backbones. Reported task results are heterogeneous.
technical.reproducibility: This activation inspected the paper tables and methods but did not run the released code. Independent replication and full matched cost accounting remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Paper-reported retriever, search-agent and memory baselines using the stated backbones; a matched total index-optimization budget was not established here.

brief.title: SELF-INDEX reports search and memory retrieval gains from revisable keys
brief.why_it_matters: Retrieval is a central bottleneck for agents that need to use growing stores of prior work. Revising retrieval keys could improve access to relevant information, but total optimization cost and task-level failures determine whether this approach is useful in practice.
